title: Rapid incident bridge cheats and stakeholder updates
body:
Purpose and scope:
This is a lightweight / fast-to-scan draft for creating the incident bridge, running the war room, and producing short public and customer-facing updates. Goal: make it trivial for the first on-call responder to set the communication cadence, notify stakeholders, and reduce cognitive load during triage.

Document status: draft — meant for SRE review. Use this as a living cheatsheet; append short examples from real incidents below.

1) Quick-start bridge script (first 5 minutes)
- Start or join the incident bridge (Zoom/Google Meet as org standard). Put the meeting link in the incident ticket and Slack #ops-bridge.
- Post a single-line Slack message to #oncall: "incident bridge started: <link> — owning: @<oncall> — short desc: <user impact>".
- Assign roles (brief):
  - Incident lead: coordinates decisions and communications (usually the on-call).
  - Triage engineer: gathers metrics & reproducible steps (logs, traces).
  - Customer comms / PM liaison: drafts public lines and escalates to CS if needed.
  - Infrastructure lead: looks at capacity, pods, autoscale, Dedicated pools.
  - Exec/ops liaison (if Sev1): provides updates to leadership every 30 min.
- If customer-visible: open a status page incident (see templates below).
- Create a short ticket with title prefix "INC-<short>" and link to bridge.

2) Internal war-room checklist (running)
- Confirm and write the current hypothesis (1 line): e.g., "Hypothesis: KV cache eviction on model-serving nodes causing >95th latency spikes."
- Verify scope: who/what is impacted (hosted API only? dedicated customers?)
- Capture immediate mitigation options and try fastest-first: fallback model, scale up Dedicated pool, revert recent infra deploy. Document each action and result.
- Evidence collection: top 3 queries, request ids, example logs, error rates (5m/1m). Snapshot and paste into ticket.
- Preserve artifacts: dump recent autoscaler logs, metrics URL, trace links, and the last deploy hash.
- If changes are made (config, routing), ensure rollback plan exists and someone is assigned to revert.
- Keep a running timestamped timeline in the ticket (every update -> short bullet).

3) Communication cadence & minimal content rules
- For Sev1 (customer-facing outage): updates every 15 minutes until stable, then 30 min until mitigation, then 60 min until resolved.
- For Sev2: updates every 30–60 minutes depending on impact.
- Always include three elements in each update: 1) What we know, 2) What we’re doing next, 3) Estimated next update time.
- No technical jargon in customer-facing lines (avoid internal IDs unless needed).

4) Status page templates (short, copy-paste friendly)
- Short outage (initial):
  Title: "Degraded inference latency for hosted API in us-west1"
  Impact: "Customers may see increased latency or timeouts for text generation and embeddings in us-west1."
  What we're doing: "Investigating; routing rules and Dedicated pools being validated. We will provide an update in 15 minutes."
- Ongoing work (30+ minutes):
  Title: "Partial mitigation in progress — inference requests returning to normal"
  Impact: "Most requests have returned to normal; a small subset may still experience timeouts or errors."
  What we're doing: "Applying temporary routing fallback to older model variants and monitoring error rates. Next update in 30 minutes."
- Resolved:
  Title: "Resolved — latency restored for hosted API in us-west1"
  Impact: "All customers should see normal inference performance. If you continue to experience issues, please contact support."
  What we did: "Rolled back problematic config and enabled routing fallback. Postmortem will be published."

5) Customer email / CS template (short, professional)
- Subject: "Service update: Degraded inference performance (US-West) — Incident {INC-<id>}"
- Body first line: "We experienced degraded inference performance affecting some requests in US-West region starting at 11:37 UTC."
- Short bullet summary: 1) Scope: hosted API + embeddings for customers in region. 2) Impact: intermittent latency/timeouts. 3) Mitigation: routing fallback + scaling Dedicated pools. 4) ETA for next update: 30 minutes.
- Close email when resolved with a short note of what changed and link to postmortem.

6) Slack and internal update examples (copyable)
- Initial oncall post: "INC-2026-112: Investigating increased latency in hosted API (us-west). Bridge: <link>. Roles assigned: lead=@aisha, triage=@marco. Status page ticket opened."
- 15-min update to #oncall: "Update: error rate 4% -> 12%. Hypothesis: autoscaler failing to add GPU nodes for model-v2. Action: manual scale + routing fallback started. Next update 15:50 UTC."
- Post-resolve note: "Resolved: latency normalized after scaling and routing fallback. Creating postmortem. If you observed customer impact please flag in ticket."

7) Short scripts for bridge moderators (dos and don'ts)
- Do: Keep language concise, call out blockers, enforce that only one person posts public updates (customer comms owner).
- Do: Ask for exact reproducible steps from product/triage quickly.
- Don't: Speculate publicly on root cause. Use "investigating" or "under investigation" until confirmed.

8) Rapid escalation matrix (who to page)
- If incident is affecting >10% of requests globally or any paid Dedicated pool customers: page SRE lead + infra + product-ops.
- If customer SLA is impacted or exec attention needed: page CTO, Head of Customer Success.

9) Mitigation knobs (Redwood-specific quick list)
- Model routing fallback: route to older model variant (model-v1 => model-v1-quantized)
- Prefix/KV cache flush or warm (try warm path for hot prefixes)
- Dedicated pool burst: manual scale up to N nodes (follow capacity plan and cost guardrails)
- Temporary downscale of batching (reduce batch size to lower latency)
- Fallback to regional replica (route to eu-west or us-east)

10) Post-incident checklist (before close)
- Confirm customer impact and flag customers who need follow-up.
- Ensure status page shows "resolved" and include short summary.
- Assign postmortem owner and timeline for draft (48–72h).
- Collect key artifacts: timelines, deploy hashes, relevant PRs, alerting rules that fired.

11) Postmortem prompt (starter questions)
- What happened and when?
- Customer impact and scope?
- Root cause (hypothesis vs verified)?
- What mitigation steps were taken and why did they work?
- What action items prevent recurrence? Who owns each?

12) Loose notes / open questions (to be resolved in team review)
- Should we standardize 15-min updates for all Sev2s? tradeoff noise vs trust.
- Do we want a dedicated customer-comms pager for large Dedicated customers?
- Add runbook steps for "model-quantized fallback" to infra runbooks with exact CLI commands.
- Consider a small script to auto-open status page incident with templated fields from the ticket.

Appendix: real short examples from past incidents (sanitized)
- Example update (first public): "We're investigating elevated latency for the hosted API in us-west. Some requests are timing out. We're validating routing and Dedicated capacity — next update in 15 minutes."
- Example final: "Resolved: the issue was caused by a misconfigured autoscaling policy after a deploy; we reverted the change and scaled Dedicated pools. Customers in the affected region should see normal service. Postmortem to follow."

Tagline: keep comms short, regular, and owned. Let the war-room solve the technical unknowns; let the comms owner protect external-facing clarity.

- Notes to self: turn top mitigation knobs into a single checklist in the infra runbooks (links above).
